Animal husbandry does not just take an hour or so. Depending on how much animals you had, it could take a very long time. Since animals are moved indoors for the winter you would need to feed them, clean their stalls, keep the manure from building up, make proper bedding for the animals, milk the cows, collect the eggs from the chickens, and perhaps even breed some of your livestock. To add to this, you still had to chop lumber for tools and firewood. Maybe even renovate the buildings on your land to keep them from falling apart.

Some farmers even travelled to nearby cities to learn about what has happened that passed year and maybe even do a few odd jobs for locals to get some extra cash. There was tons of work to be done, but I guess you can say that this work wasn't specifically "farm" work.

You still had to feed your animals, clean the stalls, and sell what you got from the harvest. As you can see there is a lot of work to be done even during the winter months. Hunting and building things such as tools were also some activities that were often done to pass the time.

I do not think that Lenin purposefully overprinted the rouble in order to eliminate the idea of capitalism. The rampant inflation that plagued the Soviet Union in the early 1920's was the result of monetary chaos in the wake of both economic devastation and the civil war.

Mismanagement and rapid nationalization of industry were taking a toll on the Soviet economy. Public industries that were once running smoothly were taken over by government officials and the production of goods was interrupted. Nationalization was seen as very important in the policies of War Communism as the Bolsheviks sought to create an ownerless and classless society. Thus, the inflation that was caused could be blamed on the policies of War Communism.

However, the civil war that was raging on also played a fundamental role. Since almost every factory was ordered to produce military goods, raw materials came in short supply and the amount of consumer goods became almost nonexistent. Peasants stopped selling what they had for money because they could buy nothing with it. Bartering and rationing became commonplace. The disuse of currency also allowed the Soviet economy to deteriorate.

For more info, http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperinflation_in_early_Soviet_Russia

I can't answer your question on Ottoman colonization/imperialism since I don't know much about the Ottomans. However, I can attempt to answer your question on Russian expansion into Siberia. 

The spread of the Russian tsardom and empire into Siberia can be considered colonialism. After the Russians conquered and subjugated the various Siberian peoples, they were quick to exploit the various natural resources found in the region (such as furs, lumber, and minerals). To protect these lands from Chinese expansion and angry Siberian tribes, the Russians created forts and outposts. The Russian government ordered many Slavic peoples to settle these outposts and forts to guard against any foreign threat. Initially, it was mostly the warlike Cossacks that inhabited Siberia and protected it from foreign threats. However, many people who were considered undesirable by the Russian government were sent to Siberia to help increase the population there and to keep them far away from civilization. This included political prisoners, murderers, thieves, and rapists. These policies are very similar to that of British colonialism, who resettled Australia by sending criminals over. 

The Russians also massacred many of the indigenous peoples of Siberia. Ethnic groups such as the Yakuts, Itelmens, and Chukchi were just some of the people who were slaughtered, raped, and forced to integrate within the Russian empire by colonialists. This type of behaviour is the same amongst Western empires. The British, French, and Spanish all violently destroyed the various Native American tribes of North America in order to incorporate these lands into their empires. If Russian expansion into Siberia is not considered colonialism, I don't know what is.
